content: The Smart Wheelchair Mobility Training Program (SWMTP) was implemented for four children with physical disabilities. This program focused on improving driving mobility, posture, and functional abilities, as assessed by the Adapted Powered Mobility Program assessment battery. Additionally, the program aimed to enhance inclusion, participation, and quality of life, as evaluated through qualitative feedback. Following each training session, children with cerebral palsy demonstrated improved driving skills and experienced positive psychosocial outcomes. In the United Kingdom and Australia, a study involving three children using powered wheelchairs utilized smart wheelchairs equipped with sensors and training facilities. The program focused on mobility, posture, and functional improvements, as well as inclusion, participation, and quality of life. The use of smart wheelchairs enabled the development of effective training schemes for children with severe and complex disabilities, offering flexibility and adaptability. In the United States, a case study of an adult with ataxia using a powered wheelchair involved 10 training sessions of 30 minutes each in varied environments. The training led to sustained improvements in wheelchair function, even one year after the intervention. A study in the United Kingdom focused on an elderly patient with left hemiplegia. Wheelchair transfer tasks were broken into eight steps, supported by verbal mediation (saying tasks aloud). This approach improved task performance and was suggested as an adjunct to standard physiotherapy for stroke patients with neglect. An 11-month-old infant with cerebral palsy in the United States underwent open exploration and prompted mobility training using toys, verbal prompts, and hand-over-hand joystick assistance. Over 14 consecutive weekday sessions, the infant's mobility success improved significantly. A systematic and written transfer program with verbal mediation was conducted for an adult with severe cognitive impairment and right hemisphere damage in the United States. Over 12 weeks, the program improved the patient’s ability to learn wheelchair transfers. In Canada, the Wheel-See-U Peer-Led Wheelchair Training Program was implemented for 11 older adult manual wheelchair users with various diagnoses. The program consisted of 90-minute peer-led sessions tailored to participants' goals. It significantly improved wheelchair skills performance and self-efficacy. A study in the United States involving an adult with chronic stroke and severe arm impairment demonstrated that learning to drive a bimanual wheelchair over six training sessions significantly increased speed and competence, though perceptions of effort and usefulness did not change. In Ireland, a survey of 91 healthcare professionals revealed a lack of skills and confidence in providing advanced wheelchair mobility training. The study highlighted the need for further education and training opportunities for service providers. A narrative review in the United States emphasized that therapists often receive minimal training in seating and mobility, leading to inexperienced service delivery, technology abandonment, wasted funding, and delays in equipment provision. The Smart Wheelchair Mobility Training Program (SWMTP) was found to improve driving skills and positively impact psychosocial outcomes in children with cerebral palsy. Similarly, peer-led community-based manual wheelchair training programs significantly enhanced confidence and self-efficacy among adult manual wheelchair users. In summary, various studies demonstrate the effectiveness of tailored wheelchair training programs in improving mobility, posture, function, and psychosocial outcomes across diverse populations, including children with disabilities, adults with chronic conditions, and older adults. However, gaps in training for healthcare professionals highlight the need for enhanced education and support to optimize service delivery.
